“Write freely about whatever you want.” That’s a door held open. Most of the time, writing has a job: answer this, explain that, persuade someone. Freedom is different. It isn’t the absence of constraints; it’s the chance to invent your own. So I’ll invent one: pay attention.

I want to write about attention because it’s the rarest thing we have. Not time—time is indifferent. Attention is how we make time mean something. When you give someone your full attention, you’re giving them a piece of your life you’ll never get back. That’s why it’s a form of love. When you give a task your attention, it becomes real. When you give a thought your attention, it grows roots.

I’ve been thinking about how we’re all walking around with too many open tabs. Not just on screens—inside us. We’re half-listening, half-reading, half-loving, half-resting. We’re never entirely anywhere. The result is a life that feels like a waiting room. But writing is different. Writing is a place where you have to be exactly here. The cursor blinks. It doesn’t care about your plans. It only asks: what now?

Maybe that’s why writing freely feels dangerous. It exposes what you actually notice. If I’m honest, I notice small things. The sound of rain on an air conditioner. The way a stranger holds a cup with both hands, as if it’s a small animal. The pause before someone answers a question they don’t want to answer. These things don’t matter, and that’s why they matter. They’re the texture of being alive.

We’re told to be productive, to optimize, to scale. But a life isn’t a startup. It’s a garden with weeds and volunteers, with things that grow because a bird dropped a seed. You can’t optimize a bird. You can only leave the window open.

So if I could write freely forever, I’d write about the unoptimizable. The useless. The slow. The child who asks why the moon follows the car. The old man who feeds pigeons and calls them “gentlemen.” The friend who sends you a photo of a weird cloud because it reminded them of you. These are not content. They are evidence.

I don’t know if any of this is good. But “good” is a constraint I didn’t agree to. The point of free writing is not to be good; it’s to be true for a moment. To let the mind move without a leash. To see what it brings back. Sometimes it brings back nothing. Sometimes it brings back a line you didn’t know you needed: *You are allowed to be a beginner at your own life.*

I think that’s what I want to say. Not to anyone in particular. Maybe to myself. Maybe to whoever reads this. You are allowed to be a beginner. You are allowed to change your mind. You are allowed to spend an afternoon doing something that doesn’t add up to anything. You are allowed to write freely, even if no one is grading it. Especially then.

The cursor blinks. The page is not blank anymore. It’s a small room we built together, you and I, out of attention. And now I’ll leave the window open.
